section_summary: This section details internal political developments, foreign relations, and civil-military tensions in Japan during the spring of 1934 under the Saito Cabinet. It covers the political fallout from General Sadao Araki's resignation, growing public and parliamentary resistance in the Diet against military dominance, and the moderate diplomatic course pursued by Foreign Minister Koki Hirota. Additionally, documents report on corruption scandals in the Ministry of Finance leading to the impending collapse of the Saito Cabinet, alongside palace maneuvers by Prince Saionji and Count Makino to block right-wing and fascist successors.

subfiles.about: Conclusion of a report regarding the imperial amnesty granted to prisoners in Japan.
subfiles.from: U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This concluding page outlines the scope of the imperial amnesty, noting that while major violent and military crimes were excluded, participants in the May 15 Incident received significant sentence reductions. It highlights public attention focused on commutation of death sentences to life imprisonment, including that of Tomeo Sagoya, the assassin of Premier Hamaguchi.
subfiles.title: Report on the Imperial Amnesty in Japan (Concluding Page)

subfiles.about: Document file note on a conversation between Ambassador Matsudaira and Maxwell M. Hamilton.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Hamilton)
subfiles.summary: A departmental cross-reference note recording a discussion between Japanese Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira and Maxwell M. Hamilton. Matsudaira emphasized that the rise of Foreign Minister Hirota had helped restore diplomacy to its proper position and moderated domestic right-wing tendencies.
subfiles.title: File Note on Conversation with Ambassador Matsudaira

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation between Japanese Ambassador Tsuneo Matsudaira and Maxwell M. Hamilton.
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton
subfiles.summary: Hamilton recounts a confidential tea discussion with Ambassador Matsudaira at his residence. Matsudaira observed that after two abnormal years following an abrupt swing to the Right, the political situation was normalizing under Foreign Minister Hirota, allowing moderate forces to regain control as rightist momentum waned.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Ambassador Matsudaira and Mr. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Division commentary on Obata's statements regarding General Araki's resignation.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Dooman)
subfiles.summary: Division officer Eugene H. Dooman assesses information provided by former diplomat Toru Obata to Ambassador Grew. The memorandum notes that while unofficial Japanese statements often flatter foreign listeners, Obata's explanation that Araki became unpopular with extremists as he grew less radical while in office aligns with existing intelligence.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on General Araki's Resignation

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting former Ambassador Obata's explanation for General Araki's resignation as War Minister.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on a private conversation with retired diplomat Toru Obata concerning General Araki's resignation. Obata revealed that Araki lost the confidence of younger chauvinist army officers after failing to deliver on promises of aggressive military action, using illness as a pretext to resign. Obata also described how Prince Kanin blocked the extremist General Mazaki in favor of General Hayashi, interpreting Hayashi's appointment and recent Diet debates as evidence that moderate and liberal elements were regaining ground.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 720: The Reason for General Araki's Resignation

subfiles.about: Routing slip recommending that Tokyo despatch No. 736 be read in full.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: A brief Department of State internal slip directing officers to read Embassy Tokyo's incoming despatch No. 736 of April 6, 1934, in full.
subfiles.title: Routing Slip on Tokyo Despatch No. 736

subfiles.about: Division memorandum recommending formal commendation for Tokyo despatch No. 736.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: The Far Eastern Division commends Grew's analysis of shifts in Japanese public sentiment regarding the military, proposing that an official instruction of commendation be sent to the Embassy in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Commending Tokyo Despatch No. 736

subfiles.about: Comprehensive despatch and Diet speech translations examining the Japanese public's reaction against military dominance.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a detailed survey of declining public support for the military following two years of crisis atmosphere and soaring defense budgets. He highlights the public backlash against Count Uchida's 'desperate diplomacy', the calming diplomatic influence of Koki Hirota, the replacement of General Araki by Hayashi, and growing parliamentary resistance to military interference in civilian politics. The despatch encloses translated excerpts from Diet sessions featuring sharp interpellations from parliamentarians criticizing bloated military expenditures, fascist activities, and extra-constitutional intrigues.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 736: The Military and the People of Japan (with Enclosure)

subfiles.about: Personnel notation slip concerning Third Secretary W. T. Turner.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: A departmental routing slip directing that a notation of commendation be entered onto the efficiency record of Third Secretary W. T. Turner in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Personnel Notation on W. T. Turner

subfiles.about: Instruction commending Ambassador Grew for despatch No. 736.
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: The Department of State formally acknowledges receipt of Tokyo despatch No. 736, expressing commendation for its thorough presentation and analysis of civilian-military dynamics in Japan.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 516: Commendation of Despatch No. 736
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Intelligence summary on Philippine domestic politics, regional military movements, and Japanese expansionism.
subfiles.from: Frank Parker, Major General, Commanding Philippine Department
subfiles.summary: Major General Parker reports on political factionalism in the Philippine Islands, including divisions within the Democrata Party, and reviews the organization and provincial regiments of the National Volunteers. The report compiles passenger traffic data through the Port of Manila and evaluates Japanese intelligence matters, including naval construction in the Mandated Islands, British garrison movements in Shanghai, and Japanese territorial aspirations toward the Dutch East Indies.
subfiles.title: Intelligence Report: Philippine Politics and Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Diplomatic report transmitting an analysis from Le Temps regarding the Saito Cabinet and Japanese foreign relations.
subfiles.from: Warrington Dawson, Special Assistant, Paris
subfiles.summary: Warrington Dawson transmits and summarizes an article by F. Chevallier published in the Paris newspaper Le Temps on April 23, 1934. The article reviews the unexpected endurance and parliamentary posture of the Saito Cabinet, the economic consolidation of Manchukuo, improved diplomatic ties with the United States and the USSR under Hirota, and Japanese agrarian relief policies.
subfiles.title: Special Report No. W.D. 1402: Special Correspondence of Le Temps from the Far East

subfiles.about: State Department document charge-out slip for decimal file 894.00.
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: An internal State Department charge-out slip recording the loan of file 894.00 for archival reference in February 1952.
subfiles.title: Document Charge-Out Form DS-933a

subfiles.about: Letter offering confidential insights into Japanese official thinking.
subfiles.from: Frederick Moore
subfiles.summary: Frederick Moore writes to Secretary Hull offering a personal, confidential interview to share insights on the thinking of Japanese leaders regarding relations with the United States and China. Moore cites his long experience as a foreign advisor to the Japanese Government and his past work with Charles Evans Hughes.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick Moore to Secretary Hull

subfiles.about: Letter scheduling an appointment for Frederick Moore with Secretary Hull.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck informs Frederick Moore that Secretary Hull is pleased to receive his letter of April 25 and arranges an interview at Hull's office for May 1, 1934.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Frederick Moore

subfiles.about: File note on Polish journalist Janta's observations on Japanese political conditions.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Hamilton)
subfiles.summary: A departmental cross-reference note recording a visit by Mr. Janta of the Polish Telegraph Agency and Gazeta Polska. Janta reported unfavorable domestic conditions in Japan marked by continuous friction between the armed forces and civilian business leaders.
subfiles.title: File Note on Observations of Polish Correspondent Janta

subfiles.about: Memorandum assessing General Kazunari Ugaki's political career and suitability for the premiership.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Dooman)
subfiles.summary: Dooman analyzes General Ugaki's transition from a Choshu conservative to a politically skilled, moderate administrator associated with liberal figures such as Hamaguchi and Shidehara. The memorandum evaluates his successful administration in Korea and predicts that while he may make tactical concessions to the military, an Ugaki premiership would not represent a regressive policy departure.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on General Kazunari Ugaki

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the arrest of Finance Ministry officials and potential fall of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the arrest of Vice Minister of Finance Kuroda and other officials on bribery charges threatens to topple the Saito Cabinet, which originally took power to eradicate official graft. Grew identifies General Ugaki as the most probable candidate to succeed Premier Saito, anticipating that Ministers Hirota and Hayashi would remain in any successor cabinet.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 96: Impending Collapse of the Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: Memorandum on the appointment of Baron Ikki as President of the Privy Council.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Division notes commenting on Tokyo despatch No. 776 regarding the promotion of Baron Ikki over Vice-President Hiranuma to the presidency of the Privy Council, noting historical precedents where the vice-president was bypassed.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Presidency of the Privy Council

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing the appointment of Baron Ikki as President of the Privy Council.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that following the retirement of Baron Kuratomi, Baron Kitokuro Ikki was selected as President of the Privy Council on the advice of Prince Saionji. By deliberately passing over the reactionary Vice-President Baron Hiranuma, the Genro and palace advisors aimed to check rightist influence, insulate the Throne from partisan politics, and reinforce the Saito administration.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 776: Appointment of Baron Kitokuro Ikki as President of the Privy Council

subfiles.about: File note on military pressure on the Japanese Cabinet and demands for political reforms.
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, Consul General, Nanking
subfiles.summary: A departmental cross-reference note recording a dispatch from Nanking regarding Japanese military pressure exerted on the civil government following the War Minister's resignation, including demands for fundamental state reorganization.
subfiles.title: File Note on Japanese Army Demands and Reforms

subfiles.about: File note enclosing diplomatic commentary on F. P. Miller's notes on China and Japan.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, U.S. Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: A departmental cross-reference note regarding commentary submitted by Minister Nelson Johnson and Consul General Peck on F. P. Miller's memoranda regarding contemporary conditions in China and Japan.
subfiles.title: File Note on Miller's Notes on China and Japan

subfiles.about: Instruction instructing the Tokyo Embassy to improve the volume and quality of consular political reporting.
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: The Department expresses concern that consular officers throughout Japan proper failed to submit sufficient political reports during 1933 to receive performance ratings. Grew is instructed to direct consular posts to pay closer attention to regional political developments while maintaining appropriate discretion so as not to jeopardize their local official standing.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 521: Political Reporting by Consular Officers in Japan
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the collapse of General Ugaki's candidacy for the premiership.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Grew advises the Department that General Ugaki's prospective bid to replace Viscount Saito has foundered due to entrenched opposition from army and navy factions. The Saito Cabinet appears poised to survive temporarily, though Finance Minister Takahashi may resign.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 121: Collapse of Ugaki Candidacy

subfiles.about: Memorandum assessing that Japanese foreign policy will remain fundamentally unchanged despite cabinet shifts.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck advises Secretary Hull that changes in Japanese governmental personnel will alter diplomatic tactics and timing rather than Japan's core foreign policy objectives, which remain deeply rooted in national ambition.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Continuity of Japanese Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Memorandum praising Ambassador Grew's detailed letter to Consul Prentiss Gilbert in Geneva.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck draws the attention of Under Secretary Phillips and Secretary Hull to Grew's insightful analysis sent to Consul Gilbert in Geneva, commending both officers for high-quality diplomatic reporting.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Ambassador Grew's Letter to Consul Gilbert

subfiles.about: Extensive confidential letter surveying Japanese foreign policy, civil-military rivalries, and relations with the League of Nations.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides Consul Gilbert in Geneva with an in-depth review of Japanese foreign and domestic policy. He notes that while Foreign Minister Hirota has worked to ease international tensions, the underlying ambition of Japanese continental supremacy remains fixed, as illustrated by the recent Amau declaration opposing Western aid to China. Grew examines strained relations with the Soviet Union, Japanese maneuvers regarding League of Nations advisory bodies, and the delicate struggle of elderly moderates like Saionji and Makino to prevent power from slipping entirely to reactionary militarists.
subfiles.title: Confidential Letter from Ambassador Grew to Consul Prentiss Gilbert (with Enclosure List)
subfiles.to: Prentiss B. Gilbert, U.S. Consul, Geneva

subfiles.about: Letter explaining views on communicating with moderate elements in Japan.
subfiles.from: Frederick Moore
subfiles.summary: Frederick Moore writes to Hornbeck clarifying his perspectives on U.S.-Japan diplomatic contacts, arguing that cultivating direct, sympathetic relationships with reasonable Japanese leaders is vital to countering chauvinist and militarist elements.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick Moore to Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of appointment letter sent to Frederick Moore.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: A duplicate departmental record copy of Hornbeck's letter of April 27, 1934, confirming an appointment for Frederick Moore with Secretary Hull.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Frederick Moore (Duplicate)

subfiles.about: Memorandum analyzing the Teikoku Rayon bribery scandal and potential successor cabinets.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Dooman)
subfiles.summary: Dooman reviews Tokyo despatch No. 814 concerning the financial scandal in the Ministry of Finance, which has made the Saito Cabinet's survival untenable. The analysis discusses efforts by Prince Saionji and Count Makino to avert a military regime, evaluating candidates Count Kiyoura and General Ugaki, while pointing to Finance Minister Takahashi as the key figure whose resignation would trigger the cabinet's collapse.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 814 and the Cabinet Crisis
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Detailed despatch on the internal political crisis of the Saito Cabinet, the Bank of Taiwan scandal, and palace maneuvers against fascists.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the multi-faceted crisis confronting the Saito Cabinet, including agricultural distress, silk price collapses, budget deficits, and ministerial resignations. The fatal blow arose from corrupt stock transfers of defunct Suzuki Shoten securities held by the Bank of Taiwan, culminating in the arrest of Vice Minister of Finance Kuroda. Grew describes the coordinated countermeasures taken by Prince Saionji and Count Makino to thwart a fascist takeover, including elevating Dr. Ikki over Baron Hiranuma as Privy Council President and encouraging Prince Konoe to travel to America, while examining Ugaki and Kiyoura as prospective prime ministers.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 814: Internal Political Situation in Japan
